title: Carmenère
description: A forgotten Bordeaux grape, rediscovered in Chile in 1994, with dark fruit, spice and a hint of green pepper.
L: Carmenère gives deep purple-red wines with blackberry, plum and red pepper, plus spice, paprika, tobacco and sometimes chocolate. Tannins are soft and acidity moderate, so it feels round and smooth. When not fully ripe, it shows a strong green pepper note.

Its name comes from carmin, the French for crimson, because its leaves turn bright red in autumn before falling. Carmenère is part of the Cabernet family; DNA shows it's a cross of Cabernet Franc and Gros Cabernet. Like its relatives, it has methoxypyrazines, which give green notes when grapes aren't fully ripe.
Where does Carmenère's name come from?
The crimson colour of its autumn leaves
Carmin means crimson; the leaves turn red in autumn.

Carmenère is deep coloured with a purple rim. On the nose, ripe plum and blackberry with a distinctive spicy, green or red pepper note. On the palate, it's smoother and softer than Cabernet Sauvignon, with less grip. That combination of soft tannin and peppery spice is the clue.
Carmenère usually has firmer tannins than Cabernet Sauvignon.
Not true. Carmenère is softer and rounder, with gentler tannins.
Carmenère gives plum, spice and a peppery note
Its name comes from its crimson autumn leaves
It's softer than Cabernet, with a green edge when unripe

Carmenère was once widely planted in Bordeaux, especially in the Médoc, and valued for its colour. But it suffered from coulure, poor fruit set in cool, wet springs, giving low and irregular yields. After phylloxera destroyed Bordeaux's vineyards in the late 19th century, growers didn't replant it. It almost vanished from France.

In the mid-19th century, Chilean growers brought Bordeaux cuttings, including Carmenère, before phylloxera struck. Chile's dry, warm climate suited it better than Bordeaux's. Today Chile grows about 95% of the world's Carmenère, around 10,000 hectares, especially in Colchagua, Cachapoal, Maipo and Peumo.
Match each place to its Carmenère role.
Carmenère's map shifted from France to Chile.

Small plantings remain in Bordeaux, and some were rediscovered in northern Italy, where they had been mistaken for Cabernet Franc. China also grows a grape called Cabernet Gernischt, now thought to be Carmenère. Some is planted in California and Washington.
Why did Carmenère almost disappear from Bordeaux?
Poor fruit set and phylloxera led growers not to replant it
Coulure made yields unreliable, so after phylloxera growers replanted other grapes.
Carmenère was a Bordeaux grape, lost after phylloxera
Chile grows about 95% of the world's Carmenère
Small plantings survive in Italy, China and Bordeaux
Explain why it was confused with Merlot
Explain how this changed Chilean wine

For over a century, Chilean growers thought much of their Merlot was Merlot. Vineyards often mixed the two. The wines tasted different, and some vines ripened weeks later. In 1994, French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot, studying vine leaves and shapes, identified many of these vines as Carmenère.

Carmenère and Merlot have similar leaves and bunches. But Carmenère ripens two to three weeks later. When the two were picked together, the Carmenère was often unripe, giving the green, vegetal notes that marked some Chilean Merlot. Separating them improved both wines.
Carmenère was rediscovered in Chile in ____.

Chile adopted Carmenère as its signature grape. Producers learned to pick it later, manage the canopy to expose bunches to sun and reduce pyrazines, and lower yields. In 1998, Chile officially recognised it. Today many premium Chilean wines are Carmenère or blends with Cabernet Sauvignon.
How do Chilean producers avoid green notes in Carmenère?
Picking with Merlot, earlier, caused the green notes in the first place.
Chile's Merlot was often Carmenère, identified in 1994
Carmenère ripens later, so early picking gave green notes
Chile adopted it as its signature grape

Carmenère's soft tannins and peppery spice suit grilled meat, roast pork, spicy sausages and dishes with paprika, cumin or roasted peppers. It handles mild spice better than tannic reds. In Chile, it goes with empanadas and pastel de choclo, a corn and beef pie.

Serve at 16 to 18 degrees. Most Carmenère is best within five years, when fruit is fresh. Top examples from Peumo or Apalta, often blended with Cabernet, age 10 years or more. Decanting helps young, oaked examples.
Why does Carmenère handle mildly spicy dishes well?
Its soft tannins clash less with spice
Firm tannins clash with chilli; Carmenère's soft tannins are more forgiving.
Try Carmenère with roasted red peppers or a dish with smoked paprika. The wine's own pepper and spice notes come forward.
Most Carmenère is made to age for decades.
Not true. Most is best within five years; only top examples age longer.
Carmenère suits grilled meat, peppers and mild spice
Most is best within five years
Who identified Carmenère in Chile in 1994?
Boursiquot, a French ampelographer, recognised it in vineyards thought to be Merlot.
Its history is one of loss and rediscovery.
Chile grows most of the world's Carmenère.
Carmenère belongs to the ____ family of grapes.
Carmenère is soft, plummy and peppery
It vanished from Bordeaux after phylloxera
Chile rediscovered it in 1994 and made it its own
It suits grilled meat and mild spice
